title: President of India
desc: Election, powers and role of Head of State

basic.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides that 'There shall be a President of India'?
basic.e: Article 52 states there shall be a President of India, who is the head of the Indian Union.

basic.q: The executive power of the Union is vested in the President under which Article?
basic.e: Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, exercised directly or through subordinate officers.

basic.q: The President of India is elected by members of an electoral college through which method?
o: Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote
basic.e: Article 55 prescribes election of the President by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, with voting by secret ballot.

basic.q: What is the normal term of office of the President of India?
basic.e: Under Article 56, the President holds office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office.

basic.q: What is the minimum age required to be eligible for election as President of India?
basic.e: Article 58 requires a candidate to have completed 35 years of age to be eligible for the office of President.

basic.q: The oath of office to the President is administered by whom?
basic.e: Article 60 provides that the oath of office is administered by the Chief Justice of India, or in his absence, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court available.

basic.q: In case of resignation, to whom does the President address the resignation letter?
basic.e: Article 56(1)(a) provides that the President may resign by writing under his hand addressed to the Vice-President.

basic.q: Which Article deals with the procedure for impeachment of the President?
basic.e: Article 61 lays down the procedure for the impeachment of the President for violation of the Constitution.

basic.q: Under which Article does the President have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment?
basic.e: Article 72 confers the pardoning power on the President, including in cases of death sentence and court martial.

basic.q: The ordinance-making power of the President is provided under which Article?
basic.e: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session.

basic.q: Who was the first President of India?
basic.e: Dr. Rajendra Prasad served as the first President of India from 1950 to 1962.

basic.q: Who is the only person to have served two full terms as President of India?
basic.e: Dr. Rajendra Prasad is the only President to have held office for two consecutive terms (1950-1962).

basic.q: Who became the first woman President of India?
basic.e: Pratibha Patil became the first woman President of India, serving from 2007 to 2012.

basic.q: Which body conducts the election of the President of India?
basic.e: The Election Commission of India conducts and supervises the presidential election under Article 324.

basic.q: A person is disqualified from being elected President if he/she holds any office of profit, except the office of the President, Vice-President, or which other office?
o: Governor of a state or Minister of the Union/a State
basic.e: Article 58(2) exempts the offices of Governor and Minister (Union or State) from being treated as offices of profit for presidential eligibility.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the electoral college for the President's election: 1. It consists of elected members of both Houses of Parliament. 2. It consists of elected members of Legislative Assemblies of States. 3. It consists of elected members of Legislative Councils of States. 4. It includes elected members of Legislative Assemblies of NCT of Delhi and Puducherry. Which of the statements given above are correct?
intermediate.e: The electoral college under Article 54 includes elected MPs and elected MLAs of states (and, after the 70th Amendment, of NCT Delhi and Puducherry), but excludes Legislative Council members and nominated members.

intermediate.q: Which of the following do NOT form part of the electoral college for the President's election? 1. Nominated members of Rajya Sabha 2. Nominated members of Legislative Assemblies 3. Members of Legislative Councils 4. Elected members of Lok Sabha
intermediate.e: Nominated members of Parliament/Assemblies and members of Legislative Councils are excluded from the electoral college; only elected members of both Houses of Parliament and State Assemblies participate.

intermediate.q: With reference to the value of votes of MLAs in the Presidential election, consider the following statements: 1. It depends on the population of the state. 2. It depends on the total number of elected members of the assembly. 3. The population figures used are frozen as per the 1971 census. Which of the statements given above are correct?
intermediate.e: All three statements are correct; the value of an MLA's vote is derived from the state's 1971 census population divided by the number of elected MLAs (further divided by 1000), and this base year is frozen by the Explanation to Article 55 as amended by the 84th Amendment.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about qualifications for the office of President: 1. He must be a citizen of India. 2. He must have completed 35 years of age. 3. He must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Article 58 requires qualification for election as a member of the House of the People (Lok Sabha), not the Rajya Sabha, so statement 3 is incorrect.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements about the President's veto power over ordinary bills is/are correct? 1. He can withhold assent absolutely. 2. He can return the bill for reconsideration once. 3. If Parliament re-passes the bill with or without amendments, the President must give assent.
intermediate.e: The President enjoys an absolute veto, can exercise a suspensive veto by returning a non-Money Bill once, but must assent if it is passed again by Parliament.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about a Money Bill and the President: 1. A Money Bill can only be introduced in Parliament with the prior recommendation of the President. 2. The President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Under Article 117, a Money Bill requires the prior recommendation of the President for introduction, and under the proviso to Article 111 the President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the impeachment of the President under Article 61: 1. The charge may be initiated in either House of Parliament. 2. At least half the total membership of that House must sign the notice. 3. The resolution must be passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The notice requires signatures of at least one-fourth, not half, of the total membership of that House; the other statements are correct.

intermediate.q: With respect to the President's pardoning power under Article 72 compared to the Governor's power under Article 161, which of the following is correct?
o: Only the President can grant pardon in cases involving sentence by court martial
Only the Governor can grant pardon in death sentence cases
Both have identical powers in all respects
The Governor's pardoning power extends to court martial sentences
intermediate.e: Article 72 uniquely empowers the President to pardon sentences by court martial and to grant pardon in death sentence cases; the Governor's Article 161 power does not extend to court-martial cases or to a full pardon of a death sentence.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements about the President's ordinance-making power (Article 123) is/are correct? 1. It can be exercised only when both Houses of Parliament are not in session. 2. An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament. 3. It must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate 6 weeks after reassembly unless approved.
intermediate.e: All three statements are correct; the ordinance power under Article 123 is a legislative power exercisable when Parliament is not in session, subject to parliamentary approval within six weeks of reassembly.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The President can nominate 12 members to the Rajya Sabha. 2. The President can currently nominate 2 members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The President nominates 12 members to Rajya Sabha under Article 80; the provision to nominate Anglo-Indian members to Lok Sabha (Article 331) was discontinued by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019, so statement 2 is no longer valid.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the 42nd and 44th Constitutional Amendments and the position of the President: 1. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding on the President. 2. The 44th Amendment (1978) allowed the President to send the advice back for reconsideration once. 3. After reconsideration, the President is bound to act according to the advice tendered. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: All statements are correct: the 42nd Amendment made ministerial advice binding, and the 44th Amendment introduced the right of reconsideration, after which the President must act on the advice.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements about disputes relating to the President's election is/are correct? 1. Such disputes are decided by the Supreme Court. 2. The election cannot be challenged merely on the ground of an existing vacancy in the electoral college.
intermediate.e: Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with exclusive jurisdiction over presidential election disputes, and a vacancy in the electoral college does not by itself invalidate the election.

intermediate.q: With reference to the removal of the President, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. Nominated members of Parliament can participate in voting on the impeachment resolution. 2. Nominated members do not participate in the President's election.
intermediate.e: While nominated members are excluded from the electoral college for election (Article 54), they do take part in the impeachment process under Article 61, since it is undertaken by full Parliament.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the financial powers of the President: 1. No Money Bill can be introduced in Parliament without his prior recommendation. 2. The Contingency Fund of India is at his disposal. 3. The Union Budget is laid before Parliament in his name. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: All three are correct: the President recommends Money Bills, controls the Contingency Fund of India (Article 267), and causes the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before Parliament (Article 112).

intermediate.q: If the office of the President falls vacant due to death, resignation or removal, within how much time must a fresh election be held as per Article 62?
o: No specific time limit is prescribed
intermediate.e: Article 62 requires that an election to fill a vacancy caused by death, resignation, or removal be held within six months of the occurrence of the vacancy.

advanced.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the President's pardoning power under Article 72 is subject to limited judicial review if exercised in an arbitrary, mala fide, or irrational manner?
o: Kehar Singh v. Union of India
Maru Ram v. Union of India
Epuru Sudhakar v. State of Andhra Pradesh
K.M. Nanavati v. State of Bombay
advanced.e: In Epuru Sudhakar v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2006), the Supreme Court held that the exercise of clemency power under Articles 72/161, though a constitutional prerogative, is subject to limited judicial review on grounds of mala fide or irrelevant considerations.

advanced.q: In Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1988), the Supreme Court held that:
o: The pardoning power of the President is subject to no limitation whatsoever and includes reappraisal of evidence as an appellate court would
The President while considering a mercy petition sits as a further court of appeal over the judgment
Article 72 confers a power distinct from the judicial process and its exercise is not an appellate review of the case decided by courts
The President cannot exercise the pardoning power in cases of death sentence
advanced.e: In Kehar Singh's case, the Supreme Court clarified that the President's power under Article 72 is a constitutional executive act distinct from the judicial process, and is not an exercise of appellate judicial function.

advanced.q: Which landmark case held that repeated re-promulgation of ordinances without placing them before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution?
o: D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar
A.K. Roy v. Union of India
advanced.e: In D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987), the Supreme Court held that repeated re-promulgation of ordinances without legislative approval is unconstitutional and a colourable exercise of power.

advanced.q: In Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), a seven-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held that:
o: Ordinances have permanent legal effect even after lapsing
Re-promulgation of ordinances is a valid and encouraged legislative practice
An ordinance is a temporary law, and courts can examine whether rights/liabilities created under it survive its expiry rather than assuming automatic enduring effect
The President has unlimited ordinance-making power even when Parliament is in session
advanced.e: The Constitution Bench in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that an ordinance is a temporary law and courts can examine whether rights/liabilities created under it survive its expiry, rejecting the idea of automatic enduring effect.

advanced.q: The Supreme Court's decision in Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955) is significant for laying down that:
o: The executive power of the Union is coextensive with the legislative power of Parliament and is not confined merely to execution of laws
The President can act independent of the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers
Ordinances have the same status as constitutional amendments
The Governor's discretionary powers are unlimited
advanced.e: In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, the Court held that executive power extends beyond mere law execution to include the framing of policy, and is co-extensive with the legislative power of the respective legislature.

advanced.q: In Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), the Supreme Court held that:
o: The President and Governor are formal/constitutional heads who act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers except in matters where discretion is expressly conferred
The President has unfettered discretion in all executive matters
The Council of Ministers has no role in advising the President
Only the Prime Minister, and not the entire Council of Ministers, can advise the President
advanced.e: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab reaffirmed that under the Cabinet system of government, the President/Governor is a formal head who normally acts on ministerial aid and advice.

advanced.q: Regarding the President's power to seek reconsideration of ministerial advice under the proviso to Article 74(1) (added by the 44th Amendment), which statement is correct?
o: The President can send the advice back for reconsideration any number of times
The President can send the advice back for reconsideration only once, and thereafter must act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration
The President is never bound by the reconsidered advice
This provision applies only to advice on Money Bills
advanced.e: The 44th Amendment's proviso allows the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice once, but he must act in accordance with the advice tendered after reconsideration.

advanced.q: Which of the following is an area where the President is generally understood to exercise some discretion, independent of binding ministerial advice, as per prevailing constitutional convention?
o: Appointment of the Prime Minister when no party/alliance has a clear majority in Lok Sabha, and dealing with a Council of Ministers that has lost majority support but delays resignation
Assent to all ordinary Bills passed by Parliament
Grant of pardon in every criminal case referred by any court
Appointment of all Governors without any recommendation
advanced.e: Though not codified, constitutional convention recognises limited situational discretion for the President in situations like the choice of Prime Minister in a hung Parliament or dealing with a Council of Ministers that has lost confidence but delays resignation.

advanced.q: Consider the constitutional position on the President's assent to State Bills reserved by the Governor under Article 200. Which statement correctly reflects the President's options under Article 201?
o: The President must always give assent within a fixed period of six months

The President may give assent, withhold assent, or in case of a non-Money Bill, return it for reconsideration by the State Legislature; historically there was no fixed constitutional timeline for this decision
The President has no role once a Bill is reserved by the Governor
The President can only withhold assent and cannot return the Bill
advanced.e: Under Article 201, the President may assent, withhold assent, or return a non-Money Bill for reconsideration; historically the Constitution prescribed no fixed timeline for this decision, a matter examined by bodies such as the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions.

advanced.q: The 1974 Supreme Court ruling in Shamsher Singh's case departed from the earlier reasoning in which case regarding the President's/Governor's discretionary powers?
o: Sardari Lal v. Union of India
State of Rajasthan v. Union of India
advanced.e: In Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab, a seven-judge bench held that the reasoning of the earlier three-judge bench in Sardari Lal's case regarding unfettered presidential/gubernatorial discretion did not lay down the correct constitutional position.

advanced.q: In U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi (1971), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Article 74(1) is merely directory, so the President can act without a Council of Ministers
The Council of Ministers does not cease to exist merely on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha and continues to advise the President till a new Council is formed
The Prime Minister ceases to hold office the moment the Lok Sabha is dissolved
The President can dissolve the Council of Ministers without any advice
advanced.e: The Court in U.N.R. Rao's case held that Article 74(1) is mandatory, and the Council of Ministers continues in office (as a caretaker government) even after dissolution of the Lok Sabha, until a new Council is constituted.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the difference between the President's veto over Union ordinary Bills and a State Bill reserved for his consideration is correct?
o: There is no difference; the same Article 111 procedure applies to both

Ordinary Union Bills are governed by Article 111, while Bills reserved by Governors are separately governed by Article 201, which has historically lacked a fixed decision timeline, distinguishing the two procedures
The President has no power over State Bills at all
State Bills reserved for the President always receive automatic assent after one year
advanced.e: Ordinary Union Bills are governed by Article 111, while Bills reserved by Governors for the President's consideration are separately governed by Article 201.

advanced.q: The concept of a 'pocket veto' exercised by the President refers to which of the following?
o: The President explicitly rejecting a Bill in writing
The President neither giving assent nor withholding assent nor returning the Bill, thereby keeping it pending indefinitely since no time limit is prescribed under Article 111
The Rajya Sabha vetoing a Money Bill
The President dissolving Parliament to avoid a Bill
advanced.e: A pocket veto arises because Article 111 prescribes no time limit within which the President must act on a Bill, allowing it to be kept pending indefinitely, as illustrated by the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.

advanced.q: With reference to Articles 72 and 161, in which respect do the President's pardoning powers exceed those of a Governor?
o: The President can pardon sentences imposed by court martial and can grant a full pardon in death sentence cases, whereas the Governor's power does not extend to court-martial cases or a full pardon of a death sentence
The Governor's pardoning power is wider because it covers all Union laws
Both powers are identical in every respect
Only the Governor can commute a death sentence
advanced.e: The President's Article 72 power uniquely extends to court-martial sentences and to granting full pardon in death sentence cases, a distinction consistently noted in constitutional commentary.

advanced.q: The principle that the President's 'satisfaction' under Article 123 (ordinance-making power) is largely non-justiciable but can be examined on limited grounds such as mala fide exercise has been discussed in which set of cases?
o: A.K. Roy v. Union of India, T. Venkata Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and R.K. Garg v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala alone
Golaknath v. State of Punjab alone
Minerva Mills v. Union of India alone
advanced.e: Cases such as A.K. Roy, T. Venkata Reddy, and R.K. Garg collectively established that while wide latitude is given to executive satisfaction under Article 123, it is not wholly beyond judicial scrutiny in cases of mala fide exercise.

title: Vice-President of India
desc: Election, Rajya Sabha role and presidential succession

basic.q: Which Article states 'There shall be a Vice-President of India'?
basic.e: Article 63 provides that there shall be a Vice-President of India.

basic.q: The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of which body?
basic.e: Article 64 designates the Vice-President as the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States).

basic.q: What is the term of office of the Vice-President of India?
basic.e: Article 67 fixes the term of office of the Vice-President at five years from the date he enters upon office.

basic.q: What is the minimum age required for a person to be eligible for election as Vice-President?
basic.e: Article 66(3) requires the candidate to have completed 35 years of age, same as for the President.

basic.q: To be eligible for election as Vice-President, a candidate must be qualified for election as a member of which House?
basic.e: Article 66(3) requires the candidate to be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha (Council of States), unlike the President who must be qualified for the Lok Sabha.

basic.q: Who administers the oath of office to the Vice-President?
basic.e: Article 69 provides that the oath is administered by the President, or some person appointed by him.

basic.q: Who was the first Vice-President of India?
basic.e: Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan served as the first Vice-President of India, from 1952 to 1962.

basic.q: In case of a vacancy in the office of the President, who officiates as President until a new President is elected?
basic.e: Article 65 provides that the Vice-President acts as President in case of a vacancy caused by death, resignation, removal, or otherwise.

basic.q: Which body conducts the election of the Vice-President of India?
basic.e: Like the President's election, the Vice-President's election is conducted by the Election Commission of India.

basic.q: The Vice-President's election, like the President's, is held by which method?
o: Proportional representation by single transferable vote
basic.e: Article 66 mandates election by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, with voting by secret ballot.

basic.q: Which Article allows Parliament to make provisions for the discharge of the President's functions in contingencies not provided for elsewhere in the Constitution?
basic.e: Article 70 allows Parliament to make provisions for discharge of the President's functions in contingencies not covered elsewhere in the Constitution.

basic.q: Who is the only Vice-President of India to have also served as (acting and then elected) President of India?
basic.e: V.V. Giri acted as President in 1969 after Dr. Zakir Husain's death in office, and was later separately elected as President the same year.

basic.q: Which Article provides that the salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha shall be as Parliament may by law determine?
basic.e: Article 97 provides that salaries and allowances of the Chairman/Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha and Speaker/Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha are as Parliament may by law determine.

basic.q: How many times can a person be re-elected as Vice-President of India?
o: No limit is prescribed by the Constitution
basic.e: Like the President, the Constitution places no limit on the number of times a person may be re-elected as Vice-President (Article 66).

basic.q: While acting as President, does the Vice-President continue to perform the duties of the Chairman of Rajya Sabha?
o: Yes, he performs both roles simultaneously
No, he does not perform the duties of Chairman of Rajya Sabha during that period
He performs the Chairman's duties only during the budget session
He must permanently resign as Vice-President
basic.e: During the period the Vice-President acts as President, he does not perform the duties of the office of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, which are discharged instead by the Deputy Chairman.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the electoral college for the Vice-President's election: 1. It consists of members of both Houses of Parliament. 2. It includes nominated members of Parliament. 3. It includes elected members of State Legislative Assemblies. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Unlike the President's electoral college, the Vice-President's electoral college (Article 66) consists only of members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members, and does not include State Legislature members.

intermediate.q: With reference to differences between the President's and Vice-President's electoral colleges, which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. State Legislative Assemblies participate in the President's election but not in the Vice-President's. 2. Nominated members of Parliament participate in the Vice-President's election but not in the President's election.
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct — the President's electoral college includes elected MLAs but excludes nominated members, while the Vice-President's college comprises only MPs, including nominated members.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements on the removal of the Vice-President under Article 67(b): 1. A resolution for removal can be initiated in either House of Parliament. 2. It requires at least 14 days' advance notice. 3. It must be passed by the Rajya Sabha by a majority of all its members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: A resolution for removal of the Vice-President can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha (not either House), requires 14 days' notice, and must be passed there by a majority of all its members before being agreed to by the Lok Sabha.

intermediate.q: Comparing the removal procedures of the President and Vice-President, which of the following is correct?
o: Both require a two-thirds special majority in both Houses after formal impeachment charges

The President is removed through an elaborate impeachment process (Article 61) for 'violation of the Constitution', while the Vice-President can be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha (Article 67) with no specific ground mentioned in the Constitution
The Vice-President's removal process is more elaborate than the President's
Neither can be removed before the end of their term
intermediate.e: The President's removal requires the elaborate impeachment procedure with specific grounds under Article 61, whereas the Vice-President's removal under Article 67(b) is a simpler resolution process with no specific ground mentioned in the Constitution.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Vice-President need not be a member of Parliament before assuming office. 2. On becoming Vice-President, if he was already a member of either House of Parliament, he must vacate that seat. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct — a person need not be a sitting MP to be elected Vice-President, but upon assuming office he must vacate any seat held in Parliament or a State Legislature, under Article 66(4).

intermediate.q: In which of the following situations does the Vice-President act as President? 1. Death of the President. 2. Resignation of the President. 3. Removal of the President by impeachment. 4. Temporary absence of the President due to illness.
intermediate.e: Under Article 65, the Vice-President acts as President in all these contingencies — death, resignation, removal, or when the President is unable to discharge functions due to absence, illness, or any other cause.

intermediate.q: For how long can the Vice-President act as President under Article 65 before a fresh presidential election must be held?
intermediate.e: Article 62 requires that when the Vice-President acts as President owing to a vacancy, a new President must be elected within six months of the vacancy arising.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. During the period the Vice-President acts as President, he is entitled to the salary and emoluments of the President and not of the Vice-President. 2. He acquires the powers and immunities of the President during that period. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: While acting as President, the Vice-President draws the emoluments and privileges of the President's office under Article 65(3), rather than those of the Vice-President.

intermediate.q: With respect to disputes relating to elections of the Vice-President, which body has exclusive jurisdiction to decide such disputes?
intermediate.e: Article 71 vests exclusive jurisdiction in the Supreme Court of India to decide all doubts and disputes relating to the election of the President and Vice-President.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha vis-a-vis the Vice-President? 1. The Deputy Chairman is elected by the members of the Rajya Sabha from amongst themselves. 2. The Deputy Chairman performs the duties of the Chairman's office when it is vacant or when the Vice-President is acting as President.
intermediate.e: Both are correct — the Deputy Chairman is elected by the House itself (Article 89) and steps in when the office of Chairman (i.e., the Vice-President) is vacant or when he acts as President.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Vice-President presides over joint sittings of both Houses of Parliament. 2. As Chairman of Rajya Sabha, the Vice-President does not have an original vote but can exercise a casting vote in case of a tie. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is incorrect — the Speaker of Lok Sabha, not the Vice-President, presides over joint sittings of Parliament (Article 118); as Rajya Sabha Chairman, the Vice-President has no original vote but can exercise a casting vote in case of equality.

intermediate.q: If the office of Vice-President falls vacant, who performs the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
o: The Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha
intermediate.e: When the office of Vice-President (and hence Chairman of Rajya Sabha) is vacant, the Deputy Chairman performs the duties of the Chairman.

intermediate.q: Consider the statement: 'A person cannot be elected Vice-President if he holds any office of profit under the Union or a State Government, except that of President, Governor, or Minister.' Is this correct?
o: Incorrect, since Ministers are not exempted
Incorrect, since only the office of President is exempted
Incorrect, as there is no such condition for the Vice-President
intermediate.e: Article 66(4) lays down conditions similar to the President's, exempting the offices of President, Governor, and Minister from the definition of 'office of profit' for Vice-Presidential eligibility.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about historical facts of the Vice-Presidency: 1. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan later became President of India. 2. Dr. Zakir Husain also served as Vice-President before becoming President. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both are correct — Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (1962-67) and Dr. Zakir Husain (1967-69) each first served as Vice-President before being elected President.

intermediate.q: Which of the following best describes the constitutional position of the Vice-President when acting as President?
o: He continues to function as Chairman of Rajya Sabha as well
He enjoys all the powers, immunities, and privileges of the President's office but does not perform the role of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha during that period
He has only ceremonial powers with no executive authority
He must seek approval of Parliament for every decision
intermediate.e: While acting as President, the Vice-President assumes the full powers and immunities of the President's office, and does not simultaneously perform his role as Rajya Sabha Chairman.

advanced.q: Which of the following constitutional distinctions between the removal procedures for the President and the Vice-President is correct?
o: The President's removal (impeachment) requires charges of 'violation of the Constitution' investigated by the other House, while the Vice-President's removal is by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha with no specific ground mentioned and no formal 'investigation' by the other House
The Vice-President can be impeached only by the Lok Sabha
The President and Vice-President have an identical removal procedure
The Vice-President's removal requires a two-thirds majority in both Houses following formal charges
advanced.e: The President's removal follows the elaborate quasi-judicial impeachment procedure of Article 61, while the Vice-President's removal under Article 67(b) is a straightforward legislative resolution process without formal charges or investigation.

advanced.q: Why is the Vice-President's electoral college confined only to members of Parliament and not extended to State Legislatures, unlike the President's?
o: Because the Vice-President's primary constitutional role is as ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, a Union legislative body, making his election a matter internal to Parliament, whereas the President as Head of State represents the entire federal structure
Because the Constitution treats the Vice-President as a lesser dignitary undeserving of federal representation
Because State Assemblies lack the administrative capacity to participate
There is no constitutional rationale; it is a historical drafting anomaly
advanced.e: Since the Vice-President's chief function is to chair the Rajya Sabha, a Union body, his election is restricted to Parliament's electoral college, unlike the President who as Head of State represents the entire federal polity including the States.

advanced.q: If both the offices of President and Vice-President are vacant simultaneously, who has been provided to discharge the functions of the President under arrangements made pursuant to Article 70?
o: The Chief Justice of India, as per the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 and rules framed thereunder
The Speaker of Lok Sabha automatically without any law
advanced.e: Under Article 70 read with the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, provision has been made for the Chief Justice of India (or, in his absence, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court) to discharge the functions of President when both offices are simultaneously vacant.

advanced.q: With reference to Article 68, within what time frame must an election be held to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President caused by expiration of the term?
o: The election must be completed before the expiration of the term
A fresh time limit of 6 months applies after the term expires
There is no time restriction whatsoever
It must be held within 1 year before the term's expiry
advanced.e: Article 68(1) requires that an election to fill a vacancy arising from the expiry of the Vice-President's term be completed before the expiration of the term, unlike the six-month rule for vacancies arising otherwise (death, resignation, removal) under Article 68(2).

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the constitutional silence on grounds for removing the Vice-President is most accurate?
o: The Constitution requires 'violation of the Constitution' as the sole ground, similar to the President
The Constitution does not specify any ground for removal of the Vice-President under Article 67(b), leaving it to the discretion of Parliament to decide when to pass such a resolution
The Constitution requires proven misconduct, as in the removal of judges
The removal requires the same 14-days-notice-plus-two-thirds-majority formula as impeachment
advanced.e: Unlike the President's impeachment, Article 67(b) is silent on grounds for removal of the Vice-President; it merely prescribes the procedure, leaving discretion to Parliament.

advanced.q: Which person has the unique distinction of being Vice-President, then acting President, and later being separately elected as President of India?
advanced.e: V.V. Giri, who was Vice-President, became acting President after Dr. Zakir Husain's death in 1969, resigned to contest, and was then elected President in his own right the same year.

advanced.q: Consider the statement: 'Under Article 67(b), the resolution for removal of the Vice-President requires an effective majority of the Rajya Sabha, meaning a majority of all the then members of the House, rather than merely a simple majority of members present and voting.' Is this correct?
o: Correct — an 'effective majority' (majority of all the then members) is required, not merely a simple majority of those present and voting
Incorrect — only a simple majority of members present and voting is required
Incorrect — a two-thirds majority is required
advanced.e: Article 67(b) requires the resolution to be passed by a majority of all the then members of the Rajya Sabha (an 'effective majority'), a higher threshold than a simple majority of members present and voting, before the Lok Sabha's simple-majority concurrence.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly explains why the Vice-President's oath (Article 69) does not include a pledge to 'preserve, protect and defend the Constitution', unlike the President's oath (Article 60)?
o: The Vice-President's oath under Article 69 is a general oath of office and secrecy, since his substantive constitutional guardianship role arises only when he acts as President, at which time he assumes the responsibilities of that office
There is no such difference; both oaths are identical
The Vice-President is exempt from taking any oath
The Vice-President's oath is administered by the Chief Justice rather than the President, hence the wording differs
advanced.e: The President's oath under Article 60 specifically includes the pledge to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution, reflecting his role as its guardian, whereas the Vice-President's oath under Article 69 is a simpler oath of office and secrecy, befitting his primary role as Rajya Sabha Chairman.

advanced.q: Which Act primarily governs the detailed procedural aspects (such as nomination, security deposit, and scrutiny of nominations) for the election of the President and Vice-President, supplementing the constitutional provisions?
o: The Representation of the People Act, 1951
The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952
advanced.e: The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952, along with rules framed under it, lays down the detailed procedural framework for these elections, supplementing Articles 54-71 of the Constitution.

advanced.q: Suppose a sitting Vice-President is elected President. What happens to the Vice-Presidency and how is it filled?
o: The Vice-Presidency automatically transfers to the next senior-most Rajya Sabha member
The office of Vice-President falls vacant and a fresh election under Article 68 must be conducted to fill it
The same person continues to hold both offices simultaneously
Parliament nominates a new Vice-President without an election
advanced.e: On assuming the Presidency, the incumbent vacates the office of Vice-President, creating a vacancy that must be filled through a fresh election conducted under Article 68 and the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.

advanced.q: With reference to the Vice-President's role as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, which statement correctly distinguishes his position from that of the Speaker of Lok Sabha?
o: Unlike the Speaker, who is an elected member of the House he presides over and can be removed by a resolution of that House alone, the Vice-President (as Rajya Sabha Chairman) is not a member of that House and is removable only through the Article 67 procedure applicable to the office of Vice-President
Both offices are removed by exactly the same procedure
The Vice-President is a member of the Rajya Sabha like any other MP
The Speaker cannot be removed at all during the Lok Sabha's term
advanced.e: The Vice-President, though ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha, is not a member of that House, unlike the Speaker who is an elected member of Lok Sabha; consequently, removing him from the Chairmanship requires removing him from the Vice-Presidency itself under Article 67.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements regarding the resignation of the Vice-President is correct?
o: He must resign in writing addressed to the Chief Justice of India
He must resign in writing addressed to the President of India
He can resign orally before the Rajya Sabha
He cannot resign during his term
advanced.e: Article 67(a) provides that the Vice-President may resign by writing under his hand addressed to the President, unlike the President who resigns to the Vice-President.

advanced.q: In the Indian Table (Warrant) of Precedence, where does the Vice-President rank?
o: Third, after the President and Prime Minister
Fourth, after the President, Prime Minister and Chief Justice
advanced.e: In the Warrant of Precedence, the Vice-President ranks second, immediately after the President and before the Prime Minister.

advanced.q: Consider the statement: 'A sitting member of Parliament, if elected Vice-President, is deemed to have vacated his parliamentary seat on the date he enters upon his office.' Under which provision is this given effect?
advanced.e: Article 66(4) mirrors Article 59(1) applicable to the President — it provides that the Vice-President shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or a State Legislature, and if already a member, is deemed to have vacated that seat upon entering office.

advanced.q: Why does the Constitution not provide any upper age limit or maximum number of terms for the Vice-President, mirroring the position for the President?
o: Because term-limit debates never arose for the Vice-Presidency

The framers deliberately modelled Vice-Presidential eligibility (Article 66) closely on Presidential eligibility (Article 58), reflecting a common design philosophy of not restricting re-election for either high constitutional office
Because the Vice-President is directly elected by the people, making term limits unnecessary
Because the 44th Amendment removed a pre-existing term limit
advanced.e: The framers mirrored the eligibility design of the President in Article 66 for the Vice-President — no maximum age or term-limit is prescribed for either office, allowing unlimited re-election if elected each time.

title: Prime Minister & Council of Ministers
desc: Appointment, powers and responsibility of the executive

basic.q: Which Article provides for a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President?
basic.e: Article 74 mandates a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President.

basic.q: Under which Article is the Prime Minister appointed by the President?
basic.e: Article 75(1) provides that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President, and other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.

basic.q: To whom is the Council of Ministers collectively responsible, as per Article 75(3)?
basic.e: Article 75(3) establishes that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (House of the People).

basic.q: As per Article 75(5), a Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament ceases to be a Minister at the expiration of which period?
basic.e: Article 75(5) provides that a Minister who is not an MP for a period of six consecutive months ceases to be a Minister at the expiry of that period.

basic.q: Which Constitutional Amendment Act inserted clause (1A) in Article 75, capping the size of the Council of Ministers?
basic.e: The 91st Amendment Act, 2003 inserted Article 75(1A), capping the total strength of the Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, at 15% of the total membership of the Lok Sabha.

basic.q: As per Article 75(1A), the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed what percentage of the total strength of the Lok Sabha?
basic.e: Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, caps the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.

basic.q: Who administers the oath of office and secrecy to a Minister?
basic.e: Under the Third Schedule read with Article 75(4), the President administers the oaths of office and secrecy to Ministers.

basic.q: Who was the first Prime Minister of India?
basic.e: Jawaharlal Nehru served as India's first Prime Minister, from 1947 to 1964.

basic.q: Which Article lays down the duties of the Prime Minister with respect to furnishing information to the President?
basic.e: Article 78 lays down the duties of the Prime Minister, including communicating to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration of Union affairs and proposals for legislation.

basic.q: Ministers hold office during the pleasure of whom, as per Article 75(2)?
basic.e: Article 75(2) states that Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, though by convention this is exercised on the advice of the Prime Minister.

basic.q: Which category of Ministers typically holds independent charge of a ministry or department but does not usually attend Cabinet meetings unless specially invited?
basic.e: Ministers of State with Independent Charge handle a ministry on their own but are not full Cabinet members and attend Cabinet meetings only when specially invited.

basic.q: The term 'Cabinet' was formally introduced into the text of the Constitution by which amendment?
basic.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 inserted a definition of 'Cabinet' in the Explanation to Article 352, describing it as the Prime Minister and other Cabinet-rank Ministers appointed under Article 75.

basic.q: Which of the following categories does NOT typically form part of the ministerial hierarchy within the Union Council of Ministers?
basic.e: Chief Ministers belong to State governments, not the Union Council of Ministers, which comprises Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers.

basic.q: Which Article empowers Parliament to determine the salaries and allowances of Ministers?
basic.e: Article 75(6) provides that the salaries and allowances of Ministers shall be as Parliament may by law determine.

basic.q: The Prime Minister is formally appointed by the President; however, by convention, whom does the President invite to form the government?
o: The senior-most member of the Lok Sabha
The leader of the party or coalition commanding a majority in the Lok Sabha
The leader of the Rajya Sabha
Any member nominated by the outgoing Prime Minister
basic.e: By well-established convention, the President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003: 1. It caps the size of the Union Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha. 2. A similar cap was introduced for State Councils of Ministers under Article 164(1A). Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 91st Amendment simultaneously inserted Article 75(1A) for the Union and Article 164(1A) for the States, both capping the Council of Ministers at 15% of the respective House's/Assembly's strength.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements regarding the 91st Amendment Act, 2003: 1. It amended the Tenth Schedule to remove the earlier exception allowing a 'split' of one-third of a party's members to escape disqualification. 2. It retained the exception for a 'merger' of two-thirds of a party's members. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both statements are correct; the 91st Amendment removed the 'split' provision from the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) while retaining the 'merger' (two-thirds) exception.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. A member disqualified under the Tenth Schedule for defection cannot be appointed as a Minister until the remainder of the term ends or they are re-elected. 2. This linkage was introduced by inserting clause (1B) in Article 75 via the 91st Amendment. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1B), providing that a member disqualified under the Tenth Schedule shall also be disqualified for appointment as a Minister until the end of the remainder of their term or until they are re-elected.

intermediate.q: With reference to collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers, consider the following statements: 1. If a no-confidence motion is passed against the government in the Lok Sabha, the entire Council of Ministers must resign, including Ministers who are members of the Rajya Sabha. 2. Individual ministers may publicly dissent from Cabinet decisions while remaining in office. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is correct — collective responsibility means the entire Council falls together, including Rajya Sabha ministers; statement 2 is incorrect since the doctrine requires all ministers to publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign.

intermediate.q: Which of the following statements about individual responsibility of Ministers is/are correct? 1. Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President. 2. By convention, the President exercises this 'pleasure' to remove an individual minister only on the advice of the Prime Minister.
intermediate.e: Both statements reflect the doctrine of individual responsibility — while ministers formally serve 'during the pleasure' of the President (Article 75(2)), in practice such pleasure is exercised only on the Prime Minister's advice.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about a person who is not a member of Parliament being appointed as a Minister: 1. Such an appointment is constitutionally valid. 2. The person must get elected or nominated to either House within six consecutive months of appointment, failing which they cease to be a Minister. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both are correct as per Article 75(5) — a non-member can be appointed Minister but must become a member of either House within six consecutive months.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Prime Minister must be a member of the Lok Sabha. 2. A member of the Rajya Sabha can also become Prime Minister. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: There is no constitutional requirement that the Prime Minister be a Lok Sabha member; a Rajya Sabha member can become Prime Minister, as happened with Dr. Manmohan Singh and H.D. Deve Gowda.

intermediate.q: With reference to the powers of the Prime Minister, consider the following statements: 1. He recommends the appointment of Ministers to the President. 2. He can request the resignation of a Minister or advise the President to dismiss one. 3. He allocates and reshuffles portfolios among Ministers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: All three are correct functions of the Prime Minister as head of the Council of Ministers, flowing from his position as its leader and the principal channel of communication with the President under Article 78.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the size of the Council of Ministers before the 91st Amendment: 1. There was no constitutional cap on the number of ministers. 2. The cap was introduced primarily to curb the practice of oversized ministries formed to accommodate coalition partners. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Before 2003, there was no constitutional limit, leading to oversized councils of ministers under coalition pressures; the 91st Amendment addressed this by capping the size at 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the difference between 'collective responsibility' and 'individual responsibility': 1. Collective responsibility is enforceable through a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha. 2. Individual responsibility can be enforced by the President's power to remove a specific minister on the Prime Minister's advice. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Both are correct — collective responsibility (Article 75(3)) works through confidence motions affecting the whole Council, while individual responsibility (Article 75(2)) allows removal of a single minister via presidential pleasure exercised on the Prime Minister's advice.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about the composition of the Union Council of Ministers: 1. It includes Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (Independent Charge), Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers as a matter of practice. 2. All these categories are explicitly defined and distinguished in the constitutional text. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is correct as a matter of practice, but statement 2 is incorrect — the Constitution does not explicitly define or distinguish these categories; they exist as a matter of administrative convention, with only the generic term 'Minister' used in the text.

intermediate.q: With reference to Article 74(2), which of the following is correct?
o: The advice tendered by Ministers to the President is subject to judicial review in all circumstances
Courts are barred from inquiring into what advice, if any, was tendered by Ministers to the President
Courts can summon Ministers to reveal the advice given to the President in any case
Article 74(2) was repealed by the 44th Amendment
intermediate.e: Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into what advice was tendered by Ministers to the President, though courts can still examine the material or facts on which a decision was based.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The Attorney General for India attends Cabinet meetings as a matter of right. 2. The Cabinet Secretary is a civil servant who heads the Cabinet Secretariat and assists in coordinating government business. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 2 is correct; statement 1 is incorrect, as the Attorney General does not attend Cabinet meetings as a matter of right and is not part of the Council of Ministers, though he has a right to speak in Parliament under Article 88.

intermediate.q: Which of the following bodies assists the Prime Minister and Cabinet in policy coordination but is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution?
o: Cabinet Secretariat and Prime Minister's Office (PMO)
intermediate.e: The Cabinet Secretariat and the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) are extra-constitutional bodies that support coordination and administration but find no explicit mention in the Constitution.

intermediate.q: Consider the following statements about ministerial appointments: 1. Ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. 2. The final choice of persons to be appointed as Ministers rests solely with the President, independent of the Prime Minister. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
intermediate.e: Statement 1 is correct per Article 75(1); statement 2 is incorrect since by convention and case law, the President's role is formal, and the real choice of Ministers rests with the Prime Minister.

advanced.q: In S.P. Anand v. H.D. Deve Gowda (1996), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of which situation?
o: Appointment of a Prime Minister who, at the time of appointment, was not a member of either House of Parliament, since Article 75(5) allows such a person six months to secure membership
Appointment of a Prime Minister without the President's approval
Simultaneous holding of the offices of President and Prime Minister by the same person
A Prime Minister continuing in office for more than six months without becoming an MP
advanced.e: In S.P. Anand v. H.D. Deve Gowda, the Supreme Court held that a person who is not a member of either House of Parliament can validly be appointed Prime Minister, since Article 75(5) permits such a person up to six months to become a member of either House.

advanced.q: Following the Supreme Court's ruling in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023) and the subsequent Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, the Prime Minister's role in the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner is best described as:
o: The Prime Minister alone appoints the CEC without any committee

The Prime Minister chairs a selection committee (also including a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by him and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha) that recommends names to the President for appointment
The Prime Minister has no role; only the Chief Justice of India recommends the CEC
The Rajya Sabha Chairman appoints the CEC on the Prime Minister's advice
advanced.e: The 2023 Act, enacted following the Supreme Court's directions in Anoop Baranwal's case, provides for a selection committee comprising the Prime Minister (Chairperson), the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister, to recommend the CEC/ECs for presidential appointment.

advanced.q: Which amendment explicitly made the President's obligation to act in accordance with the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers a part of the constitutional text, rather than mere convention?
advanced.e: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 amended Article 74(1) to expressly require the President to act in accordance with such advice, converting a convention into an express constitutional obligation.

advanced.q: Which subsequent amendment qualified the binding nature of ministerial advice introduced by the 42nd Amendment, by giving the President a limited power of reconsideration?
advanced.e: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 added a proviso to Article 74(1) empowering the President to require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice once, though he must act as per the reconsidered advice.

advanced.q: The Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions examined issues concerning presidential/gubernatorial discretion. Which of the following is generally recognised, by convention and such commission recommendations, as an area of Presidential discretion?
o: Assenting to all ordinary Bills passed by Parliament without exception
Selection of the Prime Minister when no single party or pre-poll alliance has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha
Appointing all Supreme Court judges independently of any process
advanced.e: A recognised area of discretion is the President's role in selecting a Prime Minister in a hung Parliament, guided by conventions such as calling the single largest party or pre-poll alliance first, subject to it demonstrating majority support.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the constitutional recognition of the 'Cabinet' is correct?
o: The Cabinet and the Council of Ministers were explicitly defined as distinct bodies throughout the original Constitution of 1950

The term 'Cabinet' was inserted into the Constitution's text (in the Explanation to Article 352) only by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, though the Cabinet system had functioned as a matter of convention since 1950
The Cabinet is a statutory body created under the Government of India Act, 1935
The Cabinet's existence was first recognised through a Supreme Court ruling rather than a constitutional amendment
advanced.e: Though the Cabinet functioned by convention from the start, the term 'Cabinet' was formally defined in the constitutional text only via the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, in the Explanation to Article 352.

advanced.q: Under Article 77, all executive action of the Government of India is expressed to be taken in whose name, and who makes rules for the allocation of business among Ministers?
o: In the name of the Prime Minister; rules made by the Cabinet Secretariat
In the name of the President; the President makes rules for the more convenient transaction of business and allocation of business among Ministers
In the name of Parliament; rules made by the Speaker of Lok Sabha
In the name of the Council of Ministers collectively; no rules are required
advanced.e: Article 77 provides that executive action is expressed to be taken in the name of the President, who also makes rules for the transaction and allocation of government business among Ministers, known as the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules.

advanced.q: With respect to the difference between 'collective responsibility' (Article 75(3)) and the convention of Cabinet confidentiality, which of the following is most accurate?
o: They are the same concept under different names

Collective responsibility means the Council stands or falls together before the Lok Sabha and its members publicly support all Cabinet decisions, while Cabinet confidentiality is the practice of not disclosing internal deliberations — related but conceptually distinct ideas
Cabinet confidentiality is explicitly guaranteed under Article 74(2) in identical terms to collective responsibility
Collective responsibility applies only during a national emergency
advanced.e: While related, collective responsibility is a constitutional accountability mechanism to the Lok Sabha, whereas Cabinet confidentiality is a conventional practice ensuring internal decision-making secrecy; Article 74(2) separately bars judicial inquiry into advice given to the President.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the interplay between Article 75(1B) (inserted by the 91st Amendment) and the Tenth Schedule is correct?
o: A person disqualified under the Tenth Schedule for defection can still be appointed a Minister immediately if the Speaker permits

Article 75(1B) bars appointment of a defector disqualified under the Tenth Schedule as a Minister from the date of disqualification till the date on which their term would have expired, or until they are re-elected, whichever is earlier
Article 75(1B) applies only to Rajya Sabha members
Article 75(1B) has been struck down by the Supreme Court as unconstitutional
advanced.e: Article 75(1B), inserted by the 91st Amendment, links ministerial eligibility with anti-defection disqualification, barring a disqualified member from becoming a Minister for the remainder of the term or until re-election.

advanced.q: Regarding judicial review of advice tendered under Article 74(1), which position best reflects the current constitutional understanding after various Supreme Court pronouncements?
o: Courts can never look into any material connected with a Council of Ministers' decision

Courts cannot inquire into what advice was given by Ministers to the President under Article 74(2), but they can examine the material or grounds on which a decision was based, to test its validity on other legal grounds
All Cabinet decisions are absolutely non-justiciable in every respect
The President's satisfaction under Article 74 is subject to the same test as judicial satisfaction
advanced.e: While Article 74(2) bars inquiry into the actual advice tendered, courts have clarified that the material underlying a decision can still be examined for legal validity, without breaching the bar on disclosing the advice itself.

advanced.q: Which of the following is an accurate distinction between the constitutional treatment of Ministers of State with independent charge and Cabinet Ministers?
o: Ministers of State with independent charge are, like Cabinet Ministers, always invited to every Cabinet meeting as a matter of right
There is no constitutional distinction at all between these categories; the distinction is purely a matter of governmental convention regarding rank, precedence, and attendance at Cabinet meetings
Ministers of State cannot head any ministry
Only Cabinet Ministers can be removed by the President
advanced.e: The Constitution mentions only 'Ministers' without distinguishing Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, or Deputy Ministers; these categories are purely a matter of administrative and political convention governing rank and Cabinet meeting attendance.

advanced.q: Which of the following illustrates the practical application of Article 75(5), which allows a non-member of Parliament to be appointed a Minister for up to six months?
o: Dr. Manmohan Singh's appointment as Finance Minister in 1991, after which he secured membership of the Rajya Sabha within the stipulated period
A situation that has never actually arisen in Indian political history
It applies only to the appointment of the Prime Minister, not other Ministers
It applies only to Ministers of State, not Cabinet Ministers
advanced.e: Instances of persons appointed as Ministers before securing parliamentary membership, and subsequently getting elected or nominated within the constitutionally mandated six-month period under Article 75(5), illustrate this provision's practical application.

advanced.q: Consider the following statements about the removal of the Council of Ministers versus removal of an individual Minister: 1. The entire Council of Ministers resigns upon losing a no-confidence vote in the Lok Sabha, which can only be moved in that House. 2. An individual Minister may be asked to resign, or be dismissed by the President on the Prime Minister's advice, without any confidence vote. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
advanced.e: Both reflect valid constitutional mechanisms — the former under the doctrine of collective responsibility enforced only in the Lok Sabha, and the latter under individual responsibility combined with the President's Article 75(2) 'pleasure' power exercised on the Prime Minister's advice.

advanced.q: Which of the following best captures the rationale behind the combined reforms of the 91st Amendment Act, 2003 (Article 75(1A)/(1B) and Tenth Schedule changes)?
o: To increase the size of coalition governments for wider representation

To check the trend of oversized Councils of Ministers formed to accommodate coalition allies, and to curb defection-driven horse-trading for ministerial berths by removing the 'split' exception and disqualifying defectors from ministerial appointment
To abolish the office of Deputy Prime Minister
To transfer the power of appointing Ministers from the President to the Speaker
advanced.e: The 91st Amendment was primarily aimed at curbing oversized coalition ministries and reducing defection-driven horse-trading for ministerial posts by tightening anti-defection provisions and linking them to ministerial eligibility.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements about the Prime Minister's tenure and removal is most accurate?
o: The Prime Minister has a fixed five-year term like the President
The Prime Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President, but in practice remains in office as long as they command the confidence/majority support of the Lok Sabha
The Prime Minister can only be removed through an impeachment process similar to the President's
The Rajya Sabha alone can remove the Prime Minister through a no-confidence motion
advanced.e: Like other Ministers, the Prime Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President under Article 75(2), but in constitutional practice this is circumscribed by continued majority support in the Lok Sabha, where alone a no-confidence motion can be moved.
